analysis.one_liner: Cuts taxes and rolls back federal disclosure, oversight, and consumer-credit rules for community banks.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 88 cosponsors from both parties but never got a hearing or a vote, dying in two House committees.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have cut federal taxes for banks with up to $5 billion in assets, exempted them from the corporate minimum tax, and freed thousands of small banks from routine examinations and reporting. It also would have let banks escape public disclosure of their home lending records, let customers sign away their three-day right to cancel certain loans, and let bank executives borrow more money from their own banks. It never moved after being sent to two House committees.
analysis.who_benefits: Small and mid-sized banks and bank holding companies. They would get a 20% income tax cut (larger in designated distressed areas), full exemption from the alternative minimum tax, optional partnership-style taxation, fewer on-site examinations, shorter regulatory reports, exemptions from home-mortgage disclosure and annual privacy notices, and freedom from Sarbanes-Oxley internal-control audits. Bank executives could borrow up to $250,000 from their own banks, and bank holding companies could carry three times more debt relative to equity while still paying dividends. Depositors with long-term certificates of deposit would pay lower tax rates, and rural borrowers might see somewhat cheaper loans because their lenders' interest income would be tax-exempt.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Community banks and bank holding companies

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the corporate income tax by 20% (up to $250,000 per bank, up to $500,000 in distressed areas) for banks with gross assets of $5 billion or less, and exempts them entirely from the corporate minimum tax.

Raises the asset thresholds for lighter-touch treatment across banking law — from $250 million to $1 billion for flexible examination schedules and less frequent Community Reinvestment Act exams, and from $10 million to $250 million for exemption from Home Mortgage Disclosure Act reporting.
Exempts banks with $1 billion or less in assets from the Sarbanes-Oxley requirement that management assess internal financial controls.

Lets banks making fewer than 100 home loans a year skip public disclosure of their lending, and lets consumers waive the three-day right of rescission when borrowing from an insured depository institution.
Excludes from lenders' taxable income the interest on loans secured by agricultural real estate, and cuts tax rates and defers income recognition on long-term certificates of deposit.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, who would fund the forgone revenue from the tax cuts, and consumers and fair-lending researchers, who would lose access to home-lending data and some ability to cancel loans within three days. Bank customers also lose the annual privacy notice when a bank's practices haven't changed.

drawbacks.text: Raising the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act exemption from $10 million to $250 million in assets (and exempting banks making fewer than 100 loans) would remove thousands of lenders from public reporting, shrinking the data communities and regulators use to detect discrimination in mortgage lending.

Authorizing consumers to waive the three-day right of rescission, and widening the refinance and home-equity-line exemptions, would let borrowers give up a core protection against high-pressure home-credit sales.

The package forgives federal revenue with no offset — tax cuts for banks, tax-exempt interest on agricultural-lending income, and higher caps on tax-exempt small-issue bonds — and lets bank executives collectively borrow up to $250,000 from their own institutions with the small-bank cap raised to cover banks up to $1 billion in assets.

Allowing small bank holding companies to carry three times more debt relative to equity while still paying dividends and getting expedited approvals would weaken the capital cushion that protects depositors.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Some parts are defensible housekeeping — letting very small banks file short-form reports and pruning genuinely redundant filings. But the bill's center of gravity is a package of unoffset tax cuts and disclosure exemptions for the banking industry. The consumer-facing provisions point the wrong way: less public data on who gets mortgage loans, and an easier path for borrowers to waive their rescission rights. On balance, the benefits flow to banks and their holding companies while the costs — lost revenue, lost transparency, weakened consumer rights — fall on the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to two House committees on the same day, and neither committee ever acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Jim Ryun of Kansas introduced the bill on May 3, 2005, joined by Representative Chris Cannon as an original cosponsor.
It was referred the same day to the House Financial Services Committee and the House Ways and Means Committee, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed.
It attracted 88 cosponsors — 69 Republicans and 19 Democrats — but that support never translated into committee action in the 109th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, federal revenue was not reduced by the bank tax cuts, and mortgage borrowers kept their lending-disclosure transparency and three-day cancellation rights. Banks continued paying taxes and filing the disclosures the bill would have removed.

industries.industry: Community banks and bank holding companies (under $1-5 billion in assets)
industries.note: The bill hands these banks a 20% income tax cut, minimum-tax exemption, and lighter examinations, while stripping away the public disclosure of their mortgage lending and the consumer rescission right. The industry's gains are paid for with federal revenue and reduced transparency for the communities the banks serve.

Holding companies with under $1 billion in assets would qualify for relaxed supervision and could carry 3:1 debt-to-equity (up from 1:1) while still paying dividends and getting expedited regulatory processing — more leverage with a thinner cushion protecting depositors.

industries.industry: Municipalities and small businesses using tax-exempt small-issue bonds
industries.note: Tripling the cap on qualified small-issue bonds to $30 million would let more local development projects borrow at tax-exempt rates, though the forgone federal tax revenue is the public's cost.
Lenders' interest on agricultural real estate loans would become tax-free, which could nudge rural loan rates down, but the benefit primarily accrues to the banks and costs the Treasury.

industries.industry: Bank depositors holding long-term certificates of deposit
industries.note: Interest on CDs of one year or more would be taxed at the lower capital-gains rate and deferred until maturity, a direct benefit to individual savers who hold them.
